title: Smallest degree of a Keller counterexample in dimension 3
W: In 2026 the Jacobian conjecture was refuted in three variables. The first explicit counterexample (Alpöge's map) has polynomial degree 7. Wang's theorem says degree 2 is impossible. What is the smallest degree a counterexample in three variables can have? In particular, is there one of degree 3, 4 or 5?
M: Let $d_3$ be the least $d$ such that some polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with $\max_i\deg F_i=d$ and $\det DF\in\mathbb C^\times$ is not an automorphism. Wang's theorem gives $d_3\ge3$, and Alpöge's map gives $d_3\le7$. Determine $d_3$. In particular, decide whether $d_3\le5$.
why: Once the conjecture is false in dimension 3, the main remaining question is how much room counterexamples need. Wang's quadratic theorem and the Bass–Connell–Wright cubic-homogeneous reduction both point to low degree as the decisive regime. Settling $d_3$ means either proving the conjecture for all cubic, quartic or quintic maps in three variables, which would be new even for cubics, or finding a much smaller counterexample. The answer tells us whether the phenomenon is rigid or flexible.
issues: The original 'degree 5 or less' was arbitrary, so I recast it as determining the minimal degree $d_3\in[3,7]$ and kept the $\le5$ question as the special case. Known facts: Alpöge's map (degrees 7,6,4; Jacobian -2; generically 3-to-1), a second map G (degrees 4,11,12), and Gallagher's family of every geometric degree $\ge3$ (polynomial degrees not stated in the sources I read). Wang excludes degree 2. 'Degree' must mean polynomial degree, not geometric/fibre degree, because the 2026 papers use both. The general (nonhomogeneous) cubic case in dimension 3 does not appear to be settled in the literature I found. Section 8 of arXiv:2607.20210 shows that for fixed bounded degrees, existence over an algebraically closed field is decidable by elimination. So small cases may be attackable by computation, which is a risk that this gets settled quickly. Wright's cubic-homogeneous result in dimension 3 is recalled from memory and was not re-checked. I found no source that poses the minimal-degree question explicitly. | RED TEAM: Still open: Gao (rev. Nov 4), van den Essen, Shaska, Migus, Fonollosa and de Bondt (Oct 20) give only degree>=7 maps in dim 3; de Bondt gets degree 3-6 counterexamples only in dims 4-12. No source poses d_3. M is correct, but this is a narrow refinement (JC(3,d) for 3<=d<=6), and bounded-degree search is decidable, so it may be settled by computation soon. Solid B.

title: Decidability of colouring Cayley graphs of Z^2
W: Fix a finite set D of nonzero vectors in the integer grid and join two grid points when their difference lies in D. Given D and a number of colours k, can a computer decide whether this graph can be properly coloured with k colours? On the line the answer is yes, because a colouring exists only if a periodic one does. In the plane the colourings form a tiling-type system that might have only non-periodic members.
M: For finite symmetric $D\subset\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}$ let $G_D=\mathrm{Cay}(\mathbb Z^2,D)$. (a) Is the set $\{(D,k):\chi(G_D)\le k\}$ decidable? (b) Does every $k$-colourable $G_D$ admit a proper $k$-colouring that is invariant under some finite-index subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$? A positive answer to (b) implies a positive answer to (a), since non-colourability is witnessed by a finite box (compactness) and periodic colourings can be enumerated. A negative answer to (b), i.e. a weakly aperiodic colouring system, would be of independent interest. Settle (a) or (b).
why: The k-colourings of G_D form a 2-dimensional subshift of finite type of a very special kind. General 2D SFTs can be aperiodic and have an undecidable emptiness problem (Berger), whereas 1D ones always have periodic points. So the question is whether colouring constraints coming from a group-invariant graph are rigid enough to rule out aperiodicity. This mirrors the periodic tiling conjecture, which Bhattacharya proved in Z^2 and Greenfeld–Tao disproved in high dimensions.
issues: Web searches were unavailable for this item because the search budget was exhausted, so this was not checked against the literature; it may already be posed or solved (results on periodic colourings of distance graphs and on 'domino problem' reductions to colouring are plausible prior work). Fixed a logical error: the original M called (a) and (b) 'equivalent', but (b) is only sufficient for (a). A decidable answer could coexist with aperiodic colourings. I also stated the compactness argument explicitly. The k = 2 case is trivial (bipartiteness is a parity condition, which is periodic). No counterexample attempted for k >= 3.

title: L⁴ Strichartz on the surface of a cube
W: On a square torus, the L⁴ Strichartz estimate for the Schrödinger equation loses only ε derivatives (Bourgain). On general flat surfaces with cone points only a 1/4-derivative loss is known. Decide whether the cube surface, with eight cone points of angle 3π/2 that diffract waves, behaves like the torus.
M: Let $S$ be the surface of the unit cube with its flat metric, and $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian from $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\{\text{vertices}\})$. Decide whether for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C_\varepsilon$ with $\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^4([0,1]\times S)}\le C_\varepsilon\|f\|_{H^\varepsilon(S)}$ for all $f$.
why: The cube surface is an arithmetic surface with cone points. Its 'nonsingular' eigenfunctions lift to trigonometric polynomials (Greif–Kaplan–Strichartz–Wiese), but the singular ones are not explicit, and diffraction at the vertices spoils the lattice-counting proof used on the torus. Blair–Ford–Marzuola obtain a $1/p$ loss on all compact flat cone surfaces and suggest the loss is an artefact of their method. The cube is the simplest test case where arithmetic structure and diffraction compete.
issues: Sources: Blair–Ford–Marzuola Thm 1.5 gives a $H^{1/4}$ bound for p=q=4 on compact Euclidean surfaces with conical singularities, and Remark 1.3 suggests the loss is not sharp. I found no ε-loss result for any surface whose cone angles are not of the form $2\pi/k$; pillowcase-type quotients of tori are easy. I specified the Friedrichs extension and changed 'prove' to 'decide', since the truth is unclear. The estimate would force $\|\varphi\|_{L^4}\lesssim\lambda^{\varepsilon}$ for the singular eigenfunctions and needs near-coincidence counting for an irregular spectrum.

title: Critical NLS blow-up threshold on the cube surface
W: In the plane, the focusing cubic Schrödinger equation needs at least the ground-state mass to blow up. On the surface of a cube, each corner is a cone with total angle 3π/2, which can hold a 'three-quarter' ground state. So the blow-up threshold should drop to three quarters of the planar one, and the claim is that it does exactly that.
M: Let $S$ be the surface of the unit cube with its flat metric, and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\{\text{vertices}\})$. Let $Q$ be the ground state of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$, and put $m_*=\tfrac34\|Q\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2$. For $iu_t+\Delta u+|u|^2u=0$ on $S$, prove: (i) every $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*$ gives a global $H^1$ solution; (ii) for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $m_*<\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*+\varepsilon$ whose solution blows up in finite time. (Stronger, optional: blow-up data exist for every mass $m>m_*$; also decide whether there is blow-up at mass exactly $m_*$.)
why: The sharp Gagliardo–Nirenberg constant on a cone of angle alpha <= 2*pi should be (alpha/2*pi) times the planar one, with the radial Q as extremiser. If so, conical singularities lower the mass threshold for collapse, and the cube surface turns this into a clean statement with an explicit constant. A proof would test the mass-critical blow-up theory (Weinstein, Merle–Raphaël, Burq–Gérard–Tzvetkov) on singular geometries, where existing Strichartz estimates come with loss.
issues: Web searches were unavailable for this item because the search budget was exhausted; prior work I know of (Strichartz estimates on flat cones by Ford and by Blair–Ford–Marzuola) was not re-checked. Fixes: specified the self-adjoint realisation, since on 2D cones the Laplacian on functions supported away from the vertex is not essentially self-adjoint because of the log r mode. Also replaced 'blow-up for EVERY m > 3/4||Q||^2' with 'blow-up for masses arbitrarily close above m_*'. That is the honest threshold statement, while arbitrarily large blow-up mass on a compact surface needs a separate argument, so I kept it as an optional strengthening. Part (i) looks fairly routine given a sharp GN inequality on the cone (cones with angle <= 2*pi have apex-centred disks as isoperimetric optimisers, so Polya–Szego symmetrisation should work) plus a local H^1 theory. Part (ii), building near-threshold blow-up concentrating at a vertex, is the real content.

title: Strauss exponent for an oscillating source
W: The 3D wave equation with source |u|^p has small-data global solutions exactly when p exceeds the Strauss exponent 1+sqrt2. If the source is multiplied by cos t, the usual blow-up proofs (which need a positive source) break, and time-oscillation may cancel the source. What is the new threshold?
M: For $u_{tt}-\Delta u=\cos(t)\,|u|^p$ on $\mathbb R^{1+3}$, $p>1$, with data $(u,u_t)(0)=\varepsilon(f,g)$, $f,g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, let $p_c=\inf\{p>1:$ for all $f,g$ the solution is global for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0\}$. Determine $p_c$, and show that for $1<p<p_c$ there are $f,g$ for which global existence fails for all small $\varepsilon$ (or the lifespan is finite). Is $p_c=2$ (parametric-resonance prediction) rather than $1+\sqrt2$?
why: Strauss' conjecture (now a theorem) is a central small-data threshold for nonlinear waves; all blow-up proofs use positivity of the source, so a sign-changing time-periodic factor tests which mechanism really sets the threshold. Heuristics suggest a different answer from Strauss, governed by resonance between the forcing frequency and the waves rather than by the size of the source.
issues: Original M presupposed a sharp dichotomy exponent (existence of p_c with blow-up below and global above), which need not hold; redefined p_c as an infimum and framed the blow-up side as failure of small-data global existence (growth could be infinite-time). Heuristics: near the light cone u ~ F(r-t)/r; integrating cos t |F|^p r^{1-p} along outgoing characteristics gives oscillatory cancellation, and the second-order averaged term (cos t * sin t) also averages to 0, so the Strauss/John iteration mechanism is suppressed. But |u|^{p-1} acts as a time-periodic potential cos(t) V with V ~ r^{1-p} on the shell, producing Mathieu-type resonance at frequency 1/2 with amplification exp(c int r^{1-p} dt), divergent iff p <= 2; this suggests p_c = 2, not 1+sqrt2. Not found in literature, but the search budget ran out before a dedicated search for time-dependent oscillating coefficients (literature on g(t)|u|^p usually takes g >= 0 or of power type), so novelty is uncertain.

title: Deciding rationality of PL rotation numbers
W: A circle homeomorphism made of finitely many straight pieces, with rational break points and slopes, has a rotation number. Rational rotation numbers can be confirmed by finding a rational periodic orbit. Irrational ones occur too: Belk–Hyde–Moore found √2−1 with slopes 3/2, 2/3, 1. Is there an algorithm that always decides which case holds?
M: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of orientation-preserving PL homeomorphisms of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with finitely many rational break points, rational slopes and $f(0)\in\mathbb Q$, encoded by these data. Is $\{f\in\mathcal P:\rho(f)\in\mathbb Q\}$ decidable? (It is computably enumerable: if $\rho(f)=p/q$, the zero set of the lift $F^q(x)-x-p$ is a nonempty finite union of rational points and rational intervals.)
why: Rotation numbers of rational PL maps link Thompson-like groups $T_q$, renormalisation, and number theory. Belk–Hyde–Moore conjecture that the irrational values are quadratic when slopes are powers of one rational, and they ask about decidability for one-parameter families and for finite order in $T_q$. A decision procedure would amount to a structure theorem for when renormalisation of such maps fails to close up.
issues: Belk–Hyde–Moore (arXiv:2211.05825) give an explicit rational map with $\rho=\sqrt2-1$, refuting Calegari's question. Their Questions 3–4 are close relatives (deciding for the family $f_{q,r}$, and finite order in $T_q$) but not this exact question, and I found no paper posing it. The c.e. direction checks out. $\rho$ is computable, which only helps for a fixed candidate $p/q$. The statement is clean; I added the encoding and the c.e. justification.

title: Sofa stability
W: Baek (2024) proved that Gerver's sofa has the largest area among shapes that can be moved around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width 1. Show that any movable sofa whose area is nearly Gerver's must be nearly Gerver's sofa in shape (which in particular gives uniqueness).
M: A moving sofa is a compact connected $S\subset\mathbb R^2$ that can be moved by a continuous rigid motion from $(-\infty,0]\times[0,1]$ to $[0,1]\times(-\infty,0]$ inside $L=((-\infty,1]\times[0,1])\cup([0,1]\times(-\infty,1])$. Let $G$ be Gerver's sofa, of area $A_G\approx2.21953$. Prove that there are $C,\alpha>0$ such that every moving sofa $S$ with $|S|\ge A_G-\varepsilon$ satisfies $\min_{g}|gS\,\triangle\,G|\le C\varepsilon^{\alpha}$, the minimum over rigid motions $g$ of the plane.
why: Baek's proof gives optimality, but its abstract claims neither uniqueness nor stability. A quantitative stability inequality is the standard sharpening of an isoperimetric-type theorem, as for Bonnesen-type and Fusco-Maggi-Pratelli results, and would make the solution robust, for example for numerical verification.
issues: Original used Hausdorff distance, which is not controlled by area (zero-area appendages could change it), so it was switched to symmetric-difference area. Also defined the hallway and the class of sofas, and made C, alpha existential. Even qualitative uniqueness seems not to be stated in Baek's abstract, so the alpha-free version is already open. Technical follow-up, B.

title: Euler with reversed stretching
W: Flip the sign of the vortex-stretching term in the 3D Euler vorticity equation and keep advection and the Biot-Savart law. Do smooth solutions stay smooth forever, or can they blow up in finite time?

abla\cdot\omega_0=0$ generates a global smooth solution.
why: Advection and vortex stretching are the same size under scaling, and their competition decides regularity in 1D Euler models. In the De Gregorio, Cordoba-Cordoba-Fontelos and Okamoto-Sakajo-Wunsch models, the sign and relative weight of stretching flip the answer between blow-up and regularity (Elgindi-Jeong). This is the full 3D analogue: it isolates the sign of stretching while keeping the true nonlocal Biot-Savart structure.
issues: Fixes: (1) The reversed equation does NOT preserve div omega = 0 (one computes (d_t+u.grad)div omega = -2 d_i u_j d_j omega_i + ...), so curl u != omega in general and the system is only a model. (2) The mean of omega is not conserved (d/dt mean = -int S omega), so (-Delta)^{-1} must act on the mean-free part. I fixed M accordingly. Observation: for axisymmetric swirl-free data, div omega = 0 is preserved and r*omega_theta (not omega_theta/r as in true Euler) is transported. So omega_theta can grow as fluid moves toward the axis. This is a natural first test case, and it hints that the answer may differ from true Euler. I found no 3D paper on exactly this model, only 1D analogues.

title: Non-arithmetic tones of the cube
W: Many vibration frequencies of a cube's surface come from flat tori and are rational multiples of pi squared. Prove that at least one frequency is not of this form.
M: Let $S$ be the boundary of the unit cube $[0,1]^3$ with its intrinsic flat metric (8 cone points of angle $3\pi/2$), and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $S$. Prove that some eigenvalue of $\Delta$ is not in $\pi^2\mathbb{Q}$.
why: Flat cone surfaces whose cone angles are not of the form 2pi/k cannot be quotients of tori. Numerics show 'singular' eigenfunctions, non-smooth at the vertices, with eigenvalues that look non-arithmetic. Proving that even one of them is non-arithmetic would separate diffractive spectral geometry from lattice-arithmetic behaviour, in the simplest Platonic example.
issues: Numerical work (arXiv 1809.09909) splits cube eigenfunctions into nonsingular (torus-type) and singular ones, e.g. lambda_38 approx 8.06, with most of the spectrum singular. I found no proof of non-arithmeticity. Trace-formula and Weyl-law arguments do not obviously exclude a spectrum inside pi^2 Q with unbounded denominators, so this is genuinely transcendence-flavoured. I fixed M to specify the metric and the self-adjoint extension. Narrow but clean.

title: KdV with a cosine coefficient
W: Put a cos x in front of the cubic term of the modified KdV equation on the circle. The energy and the mean are still conserved, but the L² norm is not, and the energy no longer has a definite sign. Can smooth solutions blow up in finite time?
M: Consider $u_t+u_{xxx}+(\cos(x)\,u^3)_x=0$ on $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ with real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)$. It is Hamiltonian, $u_t=\partial_x\frac{\delta H}{\delta u}$ with $H=\int(\tfrac12u_x^2-\tfrac14\cos(x)u^4)$, and conserves $\int u$ and $H$. However, $\frac{d}{dt}\int u^2=\frac12\int\sin(x)u^4$. Decide whether every such $u_0$ yields a global smooth solution, or whether $\|u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ in finite time for some $u_0$.
why: Standard mKdV on the torus is globally well-posed because L² conservation and the L²-subcritical Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality control the energy. A spatially varying coefficient breaks the translation symmetry and so the L² law, which removes the a priori bound. Any blow-up would have to come from L² growth rather than L² concentration. That is a mechanism of real interest for inhomogeneous dispersive equations, and this is about the simplest model where it could occur.
issues: I checked the conservation laws: ∫u is a Casimir and H is the Hamiltonian, while d/dt||u||² = (1/2)∫ sin x u⁴, so L² can grow. The a priori estimates close only into dM/dt ≲ M³, which does not rule out blow-up. The weighted mass ∫|cos x|^{1/3}u² cancels the quartic term in the Kato identity, but that weight is singular at the zeros of cos, so it gives no global bound. Numerics (Fourier, N=512, integrating-factor RK4, dt=1e-5, initial data 3exp(-4(x-π/2)²)) conserve H=11.28 to 4 digits while ||u||² grows from 6.4 to 12.7 by t=0.8. The coarser run dt=2e-5 reached 23.9 at t=1.0 and then lost resolution. That growth is consistent with blow-up but does not establish it. Cos x is one arbitrary choice, and the same question makes sense for any sign-changing smooth coefficient a(x). I could not finish the literature check because the web-search budget ran out; work on inhomogeneous gKdV exists, but I could not check whether this case is covered.
